mainEntity.name: Does implant surface texture make a significant difference to healing outcomes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Research suggests that implant surface texture does meaningfully influence the early stages of osseointegration. Textured surfaces have been shown in multiple studies to support greater bone-to-implant contact compared to smooth, machined surfaces. However, surface texture is one component within a wider clinical picture that includes bone quality, patient health, surgical technique, and post-operative care. Any discussion of expected outcomes should take place during a personalised clinical consultation.

mainEntity.name: How long does osseointegration typically take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Osseointegration timescales vary between individuals and depend on factors including bone density, overall health, and implant location within the mouth. In many cases, integration is considered sufficiently advanced after approximately eight to twelve weeks, though some cases may take longer. Your dental clinician will monitor healing progress and advise when it is appropriate to move forward with restoration. No fixed timeline applies to every patient, as each person's healing is unique.

mainEntity.name: Is a rougher implant surface always better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Research indicates that there is an optimal range of surface roughness that supports osseointegration in a clinically favourable way. Surfaces that are excessively rough may be more susceptible to bacterial colonisation if exposed above the bone level. Modern implant design accounts for this by applying different surface treatments to different zones of the implant — rougher surfaces where bone integration is needed, and smoother surfaces at the gum interface. The most appropriate implant design for a given patient is determined during clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can I have dental implants if I have experienced bone loss?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bone loss in the jaw, which can occur following tooth extraction or as a result of gum disease, does not automatically preclude implant treatment. In some cases, bone grafting procedures may be used to rebuild sufficient bone volume prior to implant placement. The feasibility of this depends on individual factors including the extent of bone loss and overall health. A thorough clinical and radiographic assessment is required to determine whether implants are suitable in your specific situation.

mainEntity.name: What can I do to support healing after implant placement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Following dental implant placement, your dental team will provide specific aftercare instructions tailored to your situation. General guidance typically includes: avoiding smoking, maintaining gentle oral hygiene around the surgical site, following any dietary advice provided during the immediate recovery period, attending follow-up appointments as scheduled, and contacting your practice promptly if you have concerns. Adhering to professional aftercare guidance is one of the most important contributions you can make to your own healing process.

mainEntity.name: Are dental implants suitable for everyone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implants are a well-established tooth replacement option, but they are not universally suitable for every patient. Suitability depends on factors including jawbone volume and density, systemic health conditions, medication history, oral hygiene standards, and lifestyle factors such as smoking. A comprehensive clinical assessment — including examination and appropriate imaging — is required to determine whether implants are appropriate for a given individual. Your dental clinician will discuss all relevant factors and alternative options with you during consultation.
